title: 2026-06-29-pegasus-health-onprem-network-hardening-and-audit-prep
summary: Deep dive on Pegasus Health's on-prem private deployment needs. Covered network zoning, egress proxy, customer-managed KMS options (CloudHSM vs HSM appliance), audit/alerting integration with Splunk, SSO mapping for service accounts, and SOC 2 evidence collection. Agreed next steps: run a 2-week pilot for egress testing, provide KMS architecture diagrams, and supply templates for SOC 2 control mappings.
next_steps: Redwood to send KMS architecture diagram + BYOK options (Maya) by 2026-07-02
Pegasus to share network CIDR and current firewall rule export (Ethan) by 2026-07-07
Setup pilot cluster for egress testing (schedule with Luca) - target start 2026-07-12
Provide SOC 2 evidence checklist and sample audit logs mapping (Samir) by 2026-07-05
action_items: Maya: Send private-deploy egress playbook + links to control plane docs - due 2026-07-02
Luca: Schedule pilot run and invite Pegasus infra team - due 2026-07-09
Ethan: Export current firewall rules and share topology diagram - due 2026-07-07
Samir: Produce sample Splunk ingestion mapping and example audit log payloads - due 2026-07-05
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: 64 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luca (SE), Samir (SE), Rosa (CISO), Ethan (Platform Lead), Nadia (Security Architect), Tom (Compliance)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, uh thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call, we have Pegasus security and platform on the line, and we'll focus on the on-prem private deployment questions and audit prep.
[00:18] Rosa: Thanks Maya, need to confirm we want a tight perimeter, minimal egress, and full auditability. We're SOC 2 preparing so everything needs to be demonstrable.
[00:30] Luca: Got it. We'll walk through the network zoning and egress patterns we support, plus KMS options. Quick note, transcription may garble K V cash references, sorry about that.
[00:42] Ethan: The main constraints: no direct outbound from compute nodes, everything must route through our proxy, and keys need to be customer-managed, ideally in a hardware module.
[00:55] Samir: We support BYOK via CloudHSM or customer HSM appliance for Private. We also let customers hold keys in an HSM that's on their side and we do a secure handshake for the control plane. There are a few permutations.
[01:12] Nadia: When you say control plane, is that ever exposed to internet? We need to know the minimal egress flows.
[01:20] Maya: Good question. For Redwood Private we can run a customer-managed control plane inside the VPC/on-prem; however some optional telemetry requires outbound to our ops endpoints unless you opt for air-gapped mode. We should map those exact endpoints for you.
[01:35] Rosa: Air-gapped is preferred but we need to understand the tradeoffs for maintenance and security updates. Is there a patch pipeline you can hand over?
[01:46] Luca: Yes — for air-gapped there's an offline package model and signed artifacts. For on-prem with limited egress, we support an egress proxy pattern where only a small set of endpoints are allowed.
[01:58] Tom: Also need to understand logging: we must ingest all audit logs into Splunk and retain them for two years per policy. Can Redwood ship logs or do we pull?
[02:10] Samir: Both. We can push logs into your SIEM via forwarder, or you can pull via SFTP or API. The log schema includes request metadata, model version, tokens, and actor identity. Heads up the token field is redacted by default.
[02:27] Ethan: On RBAC: we want SSO integration (SAML/SCIM) and mapping to our internal groups. Service accounts used by apps should get scoped roles, not full admin.
[02:39] Maya: We'll show role mappings and least-privilege templates. For service accounts we recommend short-lived credentials mapped to an internal service principal.
[02:51] Nadia: How's key rotation handled if we use BYOK? Our compliance requires quarterly rotation and audit trails.
[02:58] Samir: With BYOK on CloudHSM, rotation can be orchestrated via a key policy and AWS KMS lifecycle. For on-prem HSM we provide a procedure and a signed rotation step that you run; Redwood captures the rotation event in the audit log. We'll provide the signed payload examples.
[03:15] Rosa: Any additional certification artifacts you can share? We need IAM diagrams and control mappings for SOC 2 Type II.
[03:22] Maya: We'll send our SOC 2 letter and a control-mapping template that shows which Redwood control corresponds to Pegasus control objectives.
[03:30] 
[03:30] (Segue into topology discussion)
[03:35] Luca: Let me sketch the recommended network layout. Slide link in chat: https://redwood-internal.example/diagrams/private-network-layout.pdf (note - we're using an example link for artifacts).
[03:50] Luca: Suggested zones: management, inference, cache, and egress/proxy. Management hosts are put into a separate VLAN and only reachable from your bastion. Inference nodes have no direct internet; egress is via the egress gateway.
[04:05] Ethan: For egress gateway are you okay if we use a proxy that performs TLS inspection? That might conflict with healthcare regs though.
[04:12] Nadia: We try to avoid TLS inspection where PHI might be involved; prefer mTLS to enforce mutual auth.
[04:19] Samir: We support mTLS between the inference runtime and your egress proxy, and we can do header-based allow lists so payloads are restricted.
[04:30] Rosa: What's the recommended firewall policy? Stateful security groups plus NACLs?
[04:35] Luca: Typically we do security groups for east-west controls and NACLs for broader subnet-level deny lists. Use host-based firewalls on critical nodes for defense in depth.
[04:46] Tom: IDS/IPS integration? We have a network sensor and want to correlate alerts with model activity.
[04:52] Samir: We can forward flow logs and application logs to your SIEM. Also expose webhook alerting for anomalous inference patterns. We recommend hooking both network IDS and application-layer anomaly into the same Splunk index.
[05:08] (brief cross-talk)
[05:15] Rosa: What about data residency — logs and model artifacts must remain in our datacenter. Does Redwood store any persistent data outside the cluster?
[05:24] Maya: In Private mode we do not store customer data on Redwood-hosted storage. There's an optional control plane telemetry; if you disable it, nothing leaves your cluster. We will provide configuration flags that ensure no snapshot or checkpoint is sent offsite.
[05:41] Ethan: Are there any built-in protections for model parameter exfiltration? We need to assess risks where model weights or KV caches could leak.
[05:50] Luca: Model weights are read-only, stored on encrypted disks; we never transmit weights off the node unless packaging for a signed upgrade. KV cache may include prefixes of user data — we encrypt caches at rest and recommend short TTLs and strict ACLs to isolate customers.
[06:09] Nadia: Can we run inference entirely behind an internal LB with no public endpoints?
[06:13] Samir: Yes — we support internal-only load balancers and integration with your IP allow lists. The management plane can be internal-only as well.
[06:22] Rosa: For audit evidence, can you provide sample log entries and an example of a rotation record?
[06:29] Maya: Yes, Samir will produce sample payloads. We'll also provide the mapping doc for SOC 2 controls.
[06:37] (15-minute mark moved into egress specifics)
[15:02] Luca: Ok focusing on egress: many customers use an outbound proxy that terminates TLS and performs allowlisting, but as Nadia said, for PHI we prefer mTLS where the proxy only routes encrypted traf and does not inspect content.
[15:22] Ethan: We can do mTLS. Question: how does the Redwood runtime validate certificates?
[15:28] Samir: The runtime supports a local trust store and can be configured to validate via an internal CA. We also support cert rotation via your PKI and short-lived certs distributed by your SSO/PKI system.
[15:40] Rosa: If we use an HSM appliance, what's the handshake flow? Does Redwood have a connector that talks to on-prem HSM or do we mount a service?
[15:49] Luca: Two patterns: (1) Redwood connects to your HSM via a dedicated TLS tunnel with mutual auth and remote attestations; (2) a local key proxy runs in your network that signs/decrypts requests for the runtime. Pattern 2 keeps HSM traffic entirely internal to your DC.
[16:06] Ethan: For pattern 2, do we need additional software from Redwood?
[16:10] Samir: We provide a lightweight keyproxy binary with minimal dependencies, signed by Redwood. You run it behind your firewall. The runtime calls the keyproxy over mTLS and receives wrapped keys.
[16:19] Nadia: How do you attest that the binary is the right one? We need reproducible builds and a checksum.
[16:24] Maya: We'll provide signed checksums, and if needed we can do an SBOM and reproducible build artifacts.
[16:31] Tom: Back to logging retention. Does Redwood offer configurable retention for local audit stores before forwarding?
[16:36] Samir: Yes, you configure retention per index locally. Logs can be kept in the node for X days and forwarded; default is 30 days but it's fully configurable.
[16:44] Rosa: Any out-of-band admin access? Who can escalate to root?
[16:49] Luca: Escalation follows your RBAC. Redwood support requires an explicit support session and limited-time access tokens that you approve. There is no standing root access for Redwood engineers in Private unless you enable a timeframe-limited session via your admin console.
[17:05] (customer asks about emergency access)
[17:08] Maya: We have an emergency access playbook; access is logged, requires 2-man approval, and all actions are captured in audit logs. We'll attach that playbook.
[17:18] (brief pause)
[17:21] Ethan: On the topic of network blocking: can we get an allowlist of the minimal endpoints Redwood control plane needs for updates/metrics if we want partial egress?
[17:31] Maya: Yes — action item. We'll provide an endpoint list and port matrix. There are optional endpoints for telemetry — those can be disabled.
[17:40] Nadia: How are service accounts represented in logs? We want to trace back from a model call to a user or service principal.
[17:49] Samir: Each request includes an actor id, origin (IP/host), and the model version. We also include a request-id for trace correlation. If you use SSO/SCIM mapping the actor id will be your internal principal id.
[17:59] Rosa: Is there PII or PHI ever included in logs? We need to avoid storing user content unredacted.
[18:06] Luca: By default, user content is redacted in logs. You can opt in for content retention but that's discouraged for regulated workloads.
[18:15] Tom: For SOC 2 evidence, we need to show config snapshots and change history for firewall rules. Do you keep change history?
[18:23] Samir: Yes, the platform records config diffs and stores signed snapshots for a configurable period. Those snapshots can be exported as evidence.
[18:33] (crosstalk about snapshot format)
[18:40] Ethan: One more: can we run offline security scans of the container images Redwood uses?
[18:45] Maya: We'll provide SBOMs and signed artifact lists, and you can run your own scanning pipeline against the images before deploying.
[18:54] (30 minute mark - dive into pilot details)
[30:01] Luca: Proposed pilot: small cluster behind Pegasus egress proxy, single model, generate synthetic loads, verify no outbound connections other than the allowlisted endpoints, and validate log ingestion into Splunk. Duration 2 weeks.
[30:14] Ethan: That works. We'll need a playbook for onboarding and a checklist for network changes.
[30:21] Maya: We'll send the onboarding checklist and a sample ansible playbook for firewall rules.
[30:30] Nadia: About encryption in transit: does Redwood support mTLS for internal service-to-service and enable cipher suite minimums?
[30:36] Samir: Yes — mTLS everywhere supported and we default to TLS1.3 with a restricted cipher suite list.
[30:46] Rosa: Any requirement for kernel-level hardening or specific OS images?
[30:50] Luca: We recommend minimal distro images with CIS benchmarks applied. We'll share our hardened AMI/container baseline.
[31:00] (small tangent about patch windows)
[31:12] Tom: About evidence, can we get a runbook that maps Redwood's control IDs to SOC 2 criteria? We need that for our auditors.
[31:20] Maya: Yes, we'll attach a mapping doc—action item Samir.
[31:28] Ethan: One operational detail: do you support NAT sticky rules so ephemeral nodes reuse the same outbound IP for allowlisting?
[31:36] Samir: We can configure SNAT with consistent egress IPs via the egress gateway or via NAT pools so your allowlists remain stable.
[31:44] Nadia: Are there known limitations for high throughput models when running with strict egress?
[31:50] Luca: The main constraint is telemetry/metrics throughput — if you completely block metrics and telemetry, debugging is harder. But for inference throughput itself, as long as the egress gateway has enough bandwidth it's fine. We'll size accordingly.
[32:06] (40 minute mark - discussion of key rotation and HSM)
[40:05] Rosa: Let's deep-dive on KMS options. CloudHSM vs on-prem appliances?
[40:12] Samir: CloudHSM is convenient for hybrid clouds with AWS; if you're fully on-prem an HSM appliance is recommended. The appliance gives you full physical control. We support both and have integration guides for common vendors (Thales, Gemalto).
[40:26] Ethan: If we do on-prem HSM, can Redwood still sign updates? How do you verify update packages?
[40:33] Luca: All updates are signed with Redwood's code signing key and we provide verifiable signatures. You can require a chain-of-trust attestation before applying any update.
[40:43] Nadia: What about dual-control for rotations? We require two approvers for key rotation.
[40:49] Samir: We can support a dual-signature rotation flow where two authorized operators sign off on the new key before it becomes active. Rotation events are recorded in the audit log.
[40:59] Rosa: Splunk ingestion — do you accept forwarded JSON or do we need a HEC token?
[41:06] Samir: Both supported: HEC tokens are easiest, or you can forward via syslog. We'll provide sample connectors.
[41:16] Tom: For evidence, auditor may ask for a snapshot of the HSM policies. Can you produce a sample policy?
[41:23] Maya: Yes — we'll include a sample HSM policy in the KMS doc set.
[41:30] (50 minute mark - risks and mitigations)
[50:02] Ethan: Are there any common gotchas customers run into during SOC 2 audits with Redwood Private?
[50:09] Maya: Common items: missing evidence for ephemeral token rotation, not capturing config diffs, and relying on default retention. We recommend explicit retention configs and periodic export of snapshots.
[50:22] Nadia: Any known performance hit with encryption and HSM round trips for decryption?
[50:28] Luca: There's added latency for HSM ops but we use key-wrapping and cache unwrapped keys in memory with short TTLs to minimize calls. We'll provide numbers from our benchmark: typical per-request overhead under 8ms for wrapped-key flow.
[50:46] Rosa: That seems acceptable.
[50:49] Tom: Final question: can you provide a sample SOC 2 evidence bundle after pilot?
[50:55] Maya: Yes — after pilot we can produce an evidence bundle with logs, config snapshots, and the mapping doc.
[51:04] (closing minutes)
[51:10] Maya: Quick recap — Redwood to send: KMS architecture + BYOK options, endpoint allowlist, onboarding checklist, SOC 2 mapping doc, and Splunk examples. Pegasus to share firewall export and agree pilot dates.
[51:25] Ethan: We'll aim to get the firewall export and schedule the pilot.
[51:30] Rosa: Please include the signed checksum and SBOM for the keyproxy binary.
[51:36] Samir: Will do.
[51:40] (small social)
[51:45] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
[51:50] Rosa: Thanks all.
[52:00] (meeting ends - remaining time used for asynchronous Q&A in chat)

Notes on transcription: some technical acronyms may be slightly off (e.g., K V cache transcribed as K V cash), and a few names may be abbreviated. The gist of the recommendations is captured above.
